evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from ATP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: The wildtype antiviral complex and all variants bound 106-dsRNA tightly, showing dissociation constants (Kds) ranging from 0.3 to 29 nM.
source: The wildtype antiviral complex and all variants bound 106-dsRNA tightly, showing dissociation constants (Kds) ranging from 0.3 to 29 nM (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 1, and Supplementary file 1a), with only small differences in the presence or absence of ATP or with different termini.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from gel-shift assays shown in Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 1, and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: The DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 wildtype complex showed a similar gel-shift pattern for BLT and 3′ovr dsRNA.
source: The DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 wildtype complex showed a similar gel-shift pattern for BLT and 3′ovr dsRNA (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), with two prominent bands in the absence of ATP that became diffuse in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from gel-shift assays shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The wildtype complex showed two prominent bands in the absence of ATP that became diffuse in the presence of ATP.
source: The DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 wildtype complex showed a similar gel-shift pattern for BLT and 3′ovr dsRNA (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), with two prominent bands in the absence of ATP that became diffuse in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from gel-shift assays shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: These diffuse bands were not observed when ATPγS was substituted for ATP, suggesting ATP hydrolysis promotes the diffuse appearance.
source: These diffuse bands were not observed when ATPγS was substituted for ATP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), suggesting ATP hydrolysis promotes the diffuse appearance.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from gel-shift assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, with an interpretation.

claim: The addition of ATP to DCR-1•DRH-1K320A•RDE-4 did not lead to more diffuse bands, consistent with its dominant role in ATP hydrolysis.
source: These general trends were observed for gel-shift patterns using complexes containing point mutations in the helicase domain of DCR-1 or DRH-1 (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C), but consistent with its dominant role in ATP hydrolysis, the addition of ATP to DCR-1•DRH-1K320A•RDE-4 did not lead to more diffuse bands (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from gel-shift assays shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, with an interpretation.

claim: The two-band gel shifts observed with wildtype and helicase mutant complexes were not observed with the DCR-1•DRH-1 complex that lacked RDE-4.
source: The two-band gel shifts observed with wildtype and helicase mutant complexes were not observed with the DCR-1•DRH-1 complex that lacked RDE-4 (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from gel-shift assays shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The DCR-1•DRH-1 complex showed a diffuse gel-shift, suggesting the presence of RDE-4 is required for the two discrete bands observed with complexes that contained all three proteins.
source: This complex showed a diffuse gel-shift, suggesting the presence of RDE-4 is required for the two discrete bands observed with complexes that contained all three proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental result from gel-shift assays.

claim: Binding affinities under the different conditions were similar for DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 and the DCR-1G36R•DRH-1•RDE-4 complex.
source: Binding affinities under the different conditions were similar for DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 and the DCR-1G36R•DRH-1•RDE-4 complex, while affinities decreased two- to threeold for the DCR-1•DRH-1K320A•RDE-4 complex.
evidence: This is a description of the quantified experimental result from gel-shift assays.

claim: Affinities decreased two- to threefold for the DCR-1•DRH-1K320A•RDE-4 complex.
source: Binding affinities under the different conditions were similar for DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 and the DCR-1G36R•DRH-1•RDE-4 complex, while affinities decreased two- to threeold for the DCR-1•DRH-1K320A•RDE-4 complex.
evidence: This is a description of the quantified experimental result from gel-shift assays.

claim: The DCR-1•DRH-1 complex that lacked RDE-4, while still binding tightly, was 7- to 30-fold weaker than the wildtype complex, depending on the condition.
source: The DCR-1•DRH-1 complex that lacked RDE-4, while still binding tightly, was 7- to 30-fold weaker than the wildtype complex, depending on the condition.
evidence: This is a description of the quantified experimental result from gel-shift assays.

claim: For all complexes, addition of ATP decreased binding affinity.
source: For all complexes, addition of ATP decreased binding affinity.
evidence: This is a description of the quantified experimental result from gel-shift assays.

claim: For complexes that contained all three proteins, BLT dsRNA was bound slightly tighter than 3′ovr dsRNA in the presence of ATP, but terminus dependence was not observed without ATP.
source: For complexes that contained all three proteins, BLT dsRNA was bound slightly tighter than 3′ovr dsRNA in the presence of ATP, but terminus dependence was not observed without ATP.
evidence: This is a description of the quantified experimental result from gel-shift assays.

claim: The complex lacking RDE-4 showed the greatest differences in ATP and terminus dependence.
source: The complex lacking RDE-4 showed the greatest differences in ATP and terminus dependence.
evidence: This is a description of the quantified experimental result from gel-shift assays.

claim: Adding ATPγS instead of ATP decreased binding affinity further than ATP did, suggesting that ATP binding, not hydrolysis, is the primary force driving the loss of binding affinity.
source: Adding ATPγS instead of ATP decreased binding affinity further than ATP did, suggesting that ATP binding, not hydrolysis, is the primary force driving the loss of binding affinity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B, and G, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from gel-shift assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B, and G, with an interpretation.

claim: Studies of hsDcr-1 and dmDcr2 indicate ATP-independent cleavage is mediated by the Platform•PAZ domain, rather than the helicase domain.
source: Studies of hsDcr-1 and dmDcr2 indicate ATP-independent cleavage is mediated by the Platform•PAZ domain, rather than the helicase domain (Park et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2021; Sinha et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ATP-independent cleavage is lost when dsRNA termini are blocked with 2′, 3′-cyclic phosphates, suggesting this modification precludes interaction of dsRNA with the Platform•PAZ domain of DCR-1.
source: Our observation that ATP-independent cleavage is lost when dsRNA termini are blocked with 2′, 3′-cyclic phosphates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggests this modification precludes interaction of dsRNA with the Platform•PAZ domain of DCR-1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: With ATP, binding of DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 or DCR-1•DRH-1 to cyclic phosphate-blocked BLT dsRNA was similar to binding to BLT dsRNA without the cyclic phosphate block.
source: With ATP, binding of DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 or DCR-1•DRH-1 to cyclic phosphate-blocked BLT dsRNA was similar to binding to BLT dsRNA without the cyclic phosphate block (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C D, and H, and 2 H), and Kd values were nearly identical (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from gel-shift assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, D, and H.

claim: In the presence of ATP, binding is predominantly to the helicase domain of DCR-1 or DRH-1, similar to what is observed in dmDcr2.
source: This is consistent with the idea that in the presence of ATP, binding is predominantly to the helicase domain of DCR-1 or DRH-1, similar to what is observed in dmDcr2 (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the absence of ATP, DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 binds both types of BLT dsRNA with similar affinities.
source: In the absence of ATP, DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 binds both types of BLT dsRNA with similar affinities (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, compare Table 1 and Supplementary file 1a), but DCR-1•DRH-1 binds 2.5-fold better to BLT dsRNA than it does to cyclic blocked BLT dsRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F and H; compare Table 1 and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from gel-shift assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: DCR-1•DRH-1 binds 2.5-fold better to BLT dsRNA than it does to cyclic blocked BLT dsRNA in the absence of ATP.
source: In the absence of ATP, DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 binds both types of BLT dsRNA with similar affinities (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, compare Table 1 and Supplementary file 1a), but DCR-1•DRH-1 binds 2.5-fold better to BLT dsRNA than it does to cyclic blocked BLT dsRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F and H; compare Table 1 and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from gel-shift assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F and H.

claim: The 2′, 3′-cyclic phosphate blocks terminus binding to the PAZ/Platform domain but the presence of RDE-4 in the wildtype complex mutes this effect.
source: This suggests that the 2′, 3′-cyclic phosphate blocks terminus binding to the PAZ/Platform domain but the presence of RDE-4 in the wildtype complex mutes this effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from gel-shift assays.

claim: A 6.1 Å reconstruction of DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 bound to a 52-BLT dsRNA was obtained.
source: We obtained a 6.1 Å reconstruction of DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 bound to a 52-BLT dsRNA (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The density map revealed the canonical 'L shape' of Dicer.
source: Our density map revealed the canonical 'L shape' of Dicer (Lau et al., 2012; Lau et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2018; Sinha et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2022), which enabled rigid-body fitting of a human Dicer model.
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The reconstruction contained extra density at the Hel2i subdomain of the DCR-1 helicase domain, a known binding site of dsRBPs.
source: The reconstruction contained extra density at the Hel2i subdomain of the DCR-1 helicase domain, a known binding site of dsRBPs, such as human TRBP and Drosophila R2D2 (Liu et al., 2018; Yamaguchi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The extra density at the Hel2i subdomain corresponds to a single dsRBM of RDE-4.
source: Indeed, when fitting the human Dicer•TRBP model (Liu et al., 2018) into our density, the extra density was accommodated by the third dsRNA binding motif (dsRBM) of TRBP, and by analogy, we propose this density corresponds to a single dsRBM of RDE-4 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4A, based on analogy to a previous structure.

claim: Additional density was observed interacting with Dicer's helicase domain near the Hel1 subdomain.
source: In our 3D reconstructions, we also observed additional density interacting with Dicer's helicase domain near the Hel1 subdomain.
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result.

claim: AlphaFold2 models of DRH-1 NTD and helicase domains were fit into the additional density as separate rigid bodies.
source: In this density, we were able to fit AlphaFold2 models of DRH-1 NTD and helicase domains as separate rigid bodies (Figure 4A; Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach used to interpret the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The NTD of DRH-1 directly interacts with DCR-1's helicase domain.
source: These fits showed the NTD of DRH-1 directly interacting with DCR-1's helicase domain, with DRH-1's helicase and CTD domains extended away from DCR-1 and bound to the end of the 52-BLT dsRNA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DRH-1's helicase and CTD domains are extended away from DCR-1 and bound to the end of the 52-BLT dsRNA.
source: These fits showed the NTD of DRH-1 directly interacting with DCR-1's helicase domain, with DRH-1's helicase and CTD domains extended away from DCR-1 and bound to the end of the 52-BLT dsRNA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A 7.6 Å reconstruction of DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 bound to 42-BLT dsRNA was solved.
source: In a separate reconstruction, we solved DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 bound to 42-BLT dsRNA to 7.6 Å (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The 7.6 Å structure was similar to the 6.1 Å reconstruction, with the exception of additional dsRNA density bound to DCR-1.
source: This structure was similar to our 6.1 Å reconstruction, with the exception of additional dsRNA density bound to DCR-1 (compare Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The density indicates that the 42-BLT dsRNA is positioned away from the RNase III active sites.
source: We fit the human Dicer•TRBP•pre-miRNA Class 1 structure (Liu et al., 2018) as a rigid body into our complex and found that there is a slight difference in the position of the dsRNA; however, like the human Dicer structure, our density indicates that the 42-BLT dsRNA is positioned away from the RNase III active sites.
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result, compared to a previous structure.

claim: This state likely represents a pre-dicing conformation, similar to many other studies that show the importance of the PAZ domain in positioning pre-miRNA for ATP independent cleavage.
source: This state likely represents a pre-dicing conformation, similar to many other studies that show the importance of the PAZ domain in positioning pre-miRNA for ATP independent cleavage (Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM structural result, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In both reconstructions, DRH-1 was observed bound to dsRNA termini.
source: In both of our reconstructions, we observed DRH-1 bound to dsRNA termini (Figure 4A and B); however, it was still unclear how DRH-1 utilizes ATP to promote ATP-dependent cleavage.
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The dsRNA bound to DRH-1 was speculated to be trapped in an initial dsRNA binding state.
source: We speculated that the dsRNA bound to DRH-1 was trapped in an initial dsRNA binding state, because our reconstructions thus far excluded ATP and were performed in the absence of nucleotide or with ATPγS.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cryo-EM structural results.

claim: A 2.9 Å reconstruction of the helicase and CTD domains of DRH-1 bound to the middle region of the dsRNA was obtained in the presence of ATP.
source: To understand how ATP hydrolysis was coupled to cleavage, we prepared cryo-EM specimens of DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 in the presence of ATP, and added Ca2+ in addition to Mg2+ to inhibit dsRNA cleavage (see Materials and methods). Under these conditions, we obtained a 2.9 Å reconstruction of the helicase and CTD domains of DRH-1 bound to the middle region of the dsRNA, rather than its terminus (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that DRH-1 hydrolyzes ATP to translocate along dsRNA.
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: DRH-1 hydrolyzes ATP to translocate along dsRNA.
source: To understand how ATP hydrolysis was coupled to cleavage, we prepared cryo-EM specimens of DCR-1•DRH-1•RDE-4 in the presence of ATP, and added Ca2+ in addition to Mg2+ to inhibit dsRNA cleavage (see Materials and methods). Under these conditions, we obtained a 2.9 Å reconstruction of the helicase and CTD domains of DRH-1 bound to the middle region of the dsRNA, rather than its terminus (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that DRH-1 hydrolyzes ATP to translocate along dsRNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Density for DCR-1, RDE-4, and the NTD of DRH-1 was not observed in the 2.9 Å reconstruction, presumably due to increased flexibility in the presence of ATP.
source: Density for DCR-1, RDE-4, and the NTD of DRH-1 was not observed in this reconstruction, presumably due to increased flexibility in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result, with a speculative interpretation.

claim: The reconstruction showed DRH-1 in a closed conformation where Hel1, Hel2, Hel2i, and the CTD were wrapped around the dsRNA to make a network of contacts with both strands.
source: The reconstruction showed DRH-1 in a closed conformation where Hel1, Hel2, Hel2i, and the CTD were wrapped around the dsRNA to make a network of contacts with both strands (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The ATP-binding pocket at the interface of Hel1 and Hel2 contained density for ADP and Mg2+, stabilized by contacts from well conserved helicase motifs including Q, I, Ia, II, III, Va, and VI.
source: The N-terminal RecA fold (Hel1) was positioned next to the second RecA fold (Hel2). The ATP-binding pocket at the interface of these domains contained density for ADP and Mg2+, stabilized by contacts from well conserved helicase motifs including Q, I, Ia, II, III, Va, and VI (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the Hel1 subdomain, direct binding to ADP-Mg2+ involves residues from motif Q (Q297), motif I (K320 and T321), motif Ia (Q357), and motif II (D430).
source: In the Hel1 subdomain, direct binding to ADP-Mg2+ involves residues from motif Q (Q297), motif I (K320 and T321), motif Ia (Q357), and motif II (D430) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Motif Q recognizes adenine and mediates binding specificity to ATP as in other SF1 and SF2 helicases with R294's sidechain forming stacking interactions with the adenine base, in addition to the hydrogen bonds between Q297 and adenine N6 and N7.
source: Motif Q recognizes adenine and mediates binding specificity to ATP as in other SF1 and SF2 helicases with R294's sidechain forming stacking interactions with the adenine base, in addition to the hydrogen bonds between Q297 and adenine N6 and N7 (Figure 4E; Civril et al., 2011; Cordin et al., 2004; Fairman-Williams et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4E, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the Hel2 subdomain, R808 from Motif VI is positioned to make contact with the beta phosphate of the ADP molecule.
source: In the Hel2 subdomain, R808 from Motif VI is positioned to make contact with the beta phosphate of the ADP molecule.
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result.

claim: In Hel2, a conserved loop between motifs IVa and IVb was inserted into the major groove of the dsRNA.
source: In Hel2, we also found a conserved loop between motifs IVa and IVb was inserted into the major groove of the dsRNA (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), with a concomitant widening of the groove (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: The insertion of the conserved loop into the major groove was accompanied by a concomitant widening of the groove.
source: In Hel2, we also found a conserved loop between motifs IVa and IVb was inserted into the major groove of the dsRNA (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), with a concomitant widening of the groove (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: The analogous loop of MDA5 interacts with a widened major groove and is crucial for dsRNA-dependent ATP hydrolysis by MDA5.
source: The analogous loop of MDA5 interacts with a widened major groove and is crucial for dsRNA-dependent ATP hydrolysis by MDA5 (Wu et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In RIG-I, motif IVa is disordered to accommodate a 5′ppp or m7G moiety, but is observed with dsRNA containing a 5′OH, or when RIG-I is internally bound to dsRNA.
source: In RIG-I, motif IVa is disordered to accommodate a 5′ppp or m7G moiety, but is observed with dsRNA containing a 5′OH, or when RIG-I is internally bound to dsRNA (Devarkar et al., 2016; Wang and Pyle, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of this loop in RIG-I reduces ATP hydrolysis and inactivates signaling.
source: Deletion of this loop in RIG-I reduces ATP hydrolysis and inactivates signaling (Devarkar et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RIG-I's loop contains two threonine residues (T667 and T671) that when phosphorylated impair RIG-I translocation and signaling.
source: Furthermore, RIG-I's loop contains two threonine residues (T667 and T671) that when phosphorylated impair RIG-I translocation and signaling (Devarkar et al., 2018; Willemsen et al., 2017, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, see arrows pointing down).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: DRH-1's Hel2 loop has two serines (S741 and S745) that align with RIG-I's threonines, raising the possibility that DRH-1 might also be regulated by phosphorylation state.
source: Interestingly, DRH-1's Hel2 loop has two serines (S741 and S745) that align with RIG-I's threonines (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), raising the possibility that DRH-1 might also be regulated by phosphorylation state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The Hel2i subdomain is comprised of five alpha helices and is inserted between Hel2 and the CTD.
source: The Hel2i subdomain, an alpha helical insertion domain unique to RLRs and metazoan Dicers, is comprised of five alpha helices and is inserted between Hel2 and the CTD.
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result.

claim: The pincer subdomain forms the canonical V-shape that acts as a bridge connecting Hel1, Hel2, and the CTD.
source: The pincer subdomain forms the canonical V-shape that acts as a bridge connecting Hel1, Hel2, and the CTD.
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result.

claim: In the CTD, a patch of lysine residues (K987, K988, and K990) make extensive contact with phosphates in the RNA backbone.
source: In the CTD, we observed a patch of lysine residues (K987, K988, and K990) that make extensive contact with phosphates in the RNA backbone (Figure 4D and G).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4D and G.

claim: A C. elegans drh-1 null mutant animal carrying an extrachromosomal array encoding DRH-1 with point mutations K988A, W987A, and K990A, failed to rescue RNAi, suggesting these residues are key in maintaining contact with dsRNA.
source: Interestingly, Guo et al., 2013 demonstrated that a C. elegans drh-1 null mutant animal carrying an extrachromosomal array encoding DRH-1 with point mutations K988A, W987A, and K990A, failed to rescue RNAi, which suggests these residues are key in maintaining contact with dsRNA.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: K988 and W989 are conserved in RLRs, indicating these are important residues in the CTD.
source: K988 and W989 are conserved in RLRs, indicating these are important residues in the CTD (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a statement based on sequence conservation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The CTD contains a zinc structural ion that is conserved with RLRs.
source: We also found that the CTD contains a zinc structural ion that is conserved with RLRs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, see arrows pointing up, and figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structural result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and 5C.

claim: The tertiary structure of DRH-1 was well conserved with RLRs.
source: Overall, the tertiary structure of DRH-1 was well conserved with RLRs (Figure 4—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This is a description of the structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5D.

claim: The RMSD of DRH-1 to an internally bound RIG-I (PDB 7TO2) was 1.706 Å.
source: The RMSD of DRH-1 to an internally bound RIG-I (PDB 7TO2 Wang and Pyle, 2022) was 1.706 Å, while to MDA5 (PDB 4GL2 Wu et al., 2013) it was 1.708 Å.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the structural comparison.

claim: The RMSD of DRH-1 to MDA5 (PDB 4GL2) was 1.708 Å.
source: The RMSD of DRH-1 to an internally bound RIG-I (PDB 7TO2 Wang and Pyle, 2022) was 1.706 Å, while to MDA5 (PDB 4GL2 Wu et al., 2013) it was 1.708 Å.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the structural comparison.

claim: When full-length DRH-1 was purified by itself, it could not hydrolyze ATP.
source: When full-length DRH-1 was purified by itself, we found that it could not hydrolyze ATP (Figure 5A, DRH-1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from ATP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Interaction of DRH-1's NTD with DCR-1's helicase domain is considered to release DRH-1 from an autoinhibited state.
source: Since our structural studies suggested that DRH-1 translocated along dsRNA, we considered the possibility that interaction of its NTD with DCR-1's helicase domain released DRH-1 from an autoinhibited state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: This model is attractive by analogy to RIG-I, which contains two N-terminal caspase activation and recruitment domains (CARDs) involved in autoinhibition.
source: This was an attractive model by analogy to RIG-I, which contains two N-terminal caspase activation and recruitment domains (CARDs) (Figure 1A) involved in autoinhibition.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about RIG-I autoinhibition.

claim: In the absence of dsRNA, the second CARD (CARD2) interacts with RIG-I's Hel2i domain to stabilize an autoinhibited conformation and prevent signaling of an interferon response.
source: In the absence of dsRNA, the second CARD (CARD2) interacts with RIG-I's Hel2i domain to stabilize an autoinhibited conformation and prevent signaling of an interferon response (Kowalinski et al., 2011; Ramanathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the presence of its optimal substrate, a 5′ppp BLT dsRNA, RIG-I's CTD and helicase domains bind the dsRNA terminus, promoting a conformational change that disrupts the CARD2 interaction and autoinhibition.
source: In the presence of its optimal substrate, a 5′ppp BLT dsRNA, RIG-I's CTD and helicase domains bind the dsRNA terminus, promoting a conformational change that disrupts the CARD2 interaction and autoinhibition.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about RIG-I activation.

claim: RIG-I translocates along dsRNA, forms oligomers, and signals an interferon response after autoinhibition is relieved.
source: This allows RIG-I to translocate along dsRNA, form oligomers, and signal an interferon response (Devarkar et al., 2018; Peisley et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the absence of DCR-1 and RDE-4, full-length DRH-1 cannot hydrolyze ATP with dsRNA.
source: In the absence of DCR-1 and RDE-4, full-length DRH-1 cannot hydrolyze ATP with dsRNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from ATP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Deletion of DRH-1's NTD (ΔNTD DRH-1) allowed ATP hydrolysis in a terminus-dependent manner.
source: However, we found that deletion of its NTD (ΔNTD DRH-1), allowed ATP hydrolysis in a terminus-dependent manner (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental result from ATP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The NTD of DRH-1, like RIG-I's CARD domains, interacts with its own helicase domain to promote an autoinhibited state.
source: Based on these results and our structural data (Figure 4A and B), we propose that the NTD of DRH-1, like RIG-I's CARD domains, interacts with its own helicase domain to promote an autoinhibited state.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental results and structural data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: For DRH-I, binding of its NTD to DCR-1's helicase domain relieves DRH-1's autoinhibited state.
source: While binding to dsRNA relieves autoinhibition for RIG-I, for DRH-I we propose it is the binding of its NTD to DCR-1's helicase domain that relieves DRH-1's autoinhibited state (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental results and structural data shown in Figure 4.

claim: RDE-4 dampens the difference in affinity for different termini conferred by DCR-1 and/or DRH-1.
source: The DCR-1•DRH-1 complex, which lacks RDE-4, shows approximately 10-fold weaker binding for BLT dsRNA (5.18 nM) and 32-fold weaker binding (28.64 nM) for 3′ovr dsRNA, suggesting that RDE-4 dampens the difference in affinity for different termini conferred by DCR-1 and/or DRH-1 (Table 1).
